The question of whether standing desks are better for health is genuinely contested in the research. Several sources report meaningful benefits: studies cited by Healthline [d2] found standing desks reduced upper back and neck pain by 54% after 4 weeks per a CDC study, and Smithsonian [d1] notes that adults who sit two or more extra hours per day face a 125% increased risk of cardiovascular problems. WebMD [d5] similarly reports that standing desks lower risk for heart disease, obesity, and back pain, and that call center employees with standing desks were 45% more productive. An analysis of 53 studies cited by one source [d3] found 87% of workers felt more energized after just an hour of standing at work.

However, other credible sources push back strongly. Dr. Aaron Carroll of Indiana University School of Medicine states that "there's very little evidence at all that switching people from sitting to standing desks makes much of a difference on anyone's health" [d8]. The WSJ [d6] notes that the weight-loss promise of standing desks "hasn't held up in research," with calories burned standing all day equivalent to "a slice of bread." One review concludes that "we can't convincingly say that standing desks are better for you" and that they generally don't offer more orthopedic benefits than sitting desks [d9], while another source argues that claimed benefits are "overblown" and that switching between sitting and standing is "useless" [d10]. The Cleveland Clinic [d4] and WSJ [d6] suggest that the real benefit comes from movement itself, not standing, recommending alternating between sitting and standing rather than treating standing desks as a cure-all.
